dedupe_keys.name: predis disaster response decision support system validation with a serious game

description: This case study validates PREDIS, a decision support system for disaster response that predicts the human impact of a disaster, estimates the resulting needs and selects suppliers to allocate relief resources. The authors, researchers at Cranfield University and London South Bank University, ran a quasi-experiment embedded in a participatory simulation game with equal samples of 22 experts and non-experts, and compared their decisions using analytic hierarchy process weights and Borda counts; the work is published as an open-access journal article. Coverage is generic disaster scenarios; the tool uses widely available data. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence; the PREDIS model itself is not released as software. Caveats: the sample is small and the game scenarios are simulated, not live responses. The study found that PREDIS cut the time to reach decisions from the usual 72 hours after a disaster to 6 hours for experts and non-experts, and helped 71 percent of non-experts make decisions similar to those of experts. Simulation uses: an example of validating emergency supply decision models through serious games. Related records: the Houston Food Bank location-allocation study (case_study-houston-food-bank-post-disaster-location-allocation) optimises relief distribution after a disaster.
